title: Hosea 3:1–5
context: The LORD said to Hosea, “Go again, love a woman loved by another, and an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods, and love cakes of raisins.” Hosea bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley, and told her she would stay with him many days, not playing the prostitute or being with another man, and that he would be so toward her. Israel, the word explains, will live many days without king, prince, sacrifice, sacred stone, ephod, or idols, and afterward will return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and come with trembling to the LORD and to his blessings in the last days. Many readers take the woman as Gomer; chapter 3 says “a woman loved by another, and an adulteress” and does not name her.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Go again, love a woman loved by another, and an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods, and love cakes of raisins.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD said to Hosea, “Go again, love a woman loved by another, and an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods, and love cakes of raisins.” The prophet is told to love again, as the LORD loves Israel even in their turning to other gods and to cakes of raisins. The cakes are named with that turning; many readers take them as food tied to other worship, and the verse itself pairs them with other gods. The command is “Go again,” a second sending in the same figure. Many readers take the woman as Gomer; the verse does not name her.

Arminian readers hear a love that goes again after unfaithfulness, the LORD’s own love for Israel copied in the prophet’s obedience, a love that is real toward a people who have turned.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the “Go again,” the love for a woman loved by another, and the comparison “even as the LORD loves the children of Israel” as the LORD’s own appointed sign of his steadfast love.

Shared ground: the prophet is told to love as the LORD loves Israel, even while they turn to other gods. The imagery stays sober, and the woman’s name is not given in this verse.

verses.text: So I bought her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So I bought her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley.” Hosea obeys by a purchase: fifteen pieces of silver, and a homer and a half of barley. The price is told in those measures, and the verse does not explain it further. Hosea says he bought her for himself.

Arminian readers hear a costly obedience, a real sum paid to bring her home, a sign of a love that spends in order to restore, matching the LORD’s love already named.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the purchase, the silver, and the barley as the prophet’s appointed act, the sign carried out at a stated price.

Shared ground: she is bought for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley. The verse is a simple report of the price.

verses.text: I said to her, “You shall stay with me many days. You shall not play the prostitute, and you shall not be with any other man. I will also be so toward you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Hosea said to her, “You shall stay with me many days. You shall not play the prostitute, and you shall not be with any other man. I will also be so toward you.” Many days of staying, without going after another, and Hosea will be so toward her as well: a period of restraint on both sides. The “many days” of this verse prepare the “many days” of the next, when Israel is without the old supports of king and cult.

Arminian readers hear a real stretch of waiting, a shared restraint, and a word that treats the woman’s coming days as a time to stay and not to wander, a discipline that is also a keeping.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the many days, the charge not to play the prostitute or be with another man, and Hosea’s “I will also be so toward you.” as the LORD’s appointed pattern for this time, then applied to Israel.

Shared ground: many days of staying are set, and the prophet binds himself in the same period. The next verses will say what those days mean for Israel.

verses.text: For the children of Israel shall live many days without king, without prince, without sacrifice, without sacred stone, and without ephod or idols.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the children of Israel shall live many days without king, without prince, without sacrifice, without sacred stone, and without ephod or idols.” The many days are Israel’s: no king, no prince, no sacrifice, no sacred stone, no ephod or idols. Royal rule and cult are both stripped away, the illicit items (sacred stone and idols) listed with sacrifice and ephod. Many readers take the list as a time without both false worship and the ordinary means of Israel’s life before God; the verse names the absences and does not narrate a later century.

Arminian readers hear a real interval of loss, a people living through days of being without, a discipline that still has the “Afterward” of the next verse and so is not the last word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the many days without king, prince, sacrifice, sacred stone, ephod, or idols as the LORD’s appointed time for Israel, the national meaning of the prophet’s “many days.”

Shared ground: Israel will live many days without these things. The list is the verse’s own measure of the interval.

verses.text: Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and shall come with trembling to the LORD and to his blessings in the last days.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and shall come with trembling to the LORD and to his blessings in the last days.” After the many days comes a return: they will seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and come with trembling to the LORD and to his blessings in the last days. The promise of David their king stands with the LORD’s word to David in 2 Samuel 7, shared ground for both traditions, a hope of return and of a Davidic king. The verse does not open a new dispute over that covenant.

Arminian readers hear a genuine afterward, a people who return and seek, a trembling approach to the LORD and to his blessings, and a Davidic hope held out as part of that seeking, not as a slogan apart from it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the return, the seeking of the LORD their God and of David their king, and the coming with trembling in the last days as the LORD’s own sure end for the many days, his promise standing with 2 Samuel 7.

Shared ground: Israel will return and seek the LORD and David their king. 2 Samuel 7 is the shared ground of that Davidic hope, and no new contrast is drawn from it.
